title: Gusto Went to LDX3 NYC
body_markdown:
In September, Gusto attended[LDX3 NYC](https://leaddev.com/leaddev-new-york/) — a conference entirely dedicated to leadership in tech. There were managers, directors, tech leads, and senior engineers. Attendees jumped between the technical and management stage, learning about “Re-engineering the software development playbook” on the management stage one hour and “How to kill the code review” on the technical choices stage the next.


The one thing we had in common: everyone there was invested in learning how to become a better leader.


*📸 Pictured left to right: Kamilah Taylor, Vianca Martinez, Tori Huang, Rebecca Borison, Irina Khafizova, Anshuma Chandak (and Alyssa Hester here in spirit!)*


Because, of course, AI. Everything is changing and we need to adapt. Are code reviews dead? Does my team structure and processes still make sense? How do I harness the power of these new tools while maintaining (even raising) our code quality bar? What must be dismantled? Rebuilt? Protected? So many open questions. That means we need leadership now more than ever. That need doesn’t sit just at the director level. It’s at *every* level, on *every* team.


Hello 👋 I’m Tori (in the back with the white flower earrings). I’m a Senior Staff Software Engineer at Gusto, and LDX3 was one of the coolest conferences I have ever attended. I loved it — new ideas, new connections, and most importantly, meeting and learning from folks who are all navigating similar challenges.


Part of this conference, for me, was sitting in a room full of people who are also just figuring it out. There is something extremely reassuring about sitting in a talk titled “Tackling the junior developer crisis in the age of AI,” with a bunch of other engineers who are *also* concerned. Who *also* don’t know with full certainty what to do next, but who are determined to figure it out.


So here are some takeaways, from all of us Gusto attendees, on what we learned and how it will shape our work moving forward.


### Kamilah Taylor, Head of Mobile Core Engineering


I knew going in that a lot of talks would circle around AI, and I was certainly quite curious to see what the sentiment was across the industry and how others were working through different challenges. Some things that I’m reflecting on:


**Some new problems are old problems.** In many of the Director+ roundtables and discussion groups, even if the jumping off point was how is AI impacting x, we usually ended up discussing this in a very similar way as we would have pre AI. A great example of this was in the managing managers discussion, where we found that we had very similar challenges that we needed to work through when scaling our engineering leadership as we did a few years ago.


**Everyone is overwhelmed with increased volume.** Increased volume of what? Well, everything. More PRs, more docs, easier access to more data. I thought Camille Fournier’s[insights](https://skamille.medium.com/the-managers-path-in-the-age-of-ai-279cb6611d66) here were especially interesting — there’s a huge temptation to just always ask AI for data or summaries. “Visibility is up but understanding is not.” We still need to exercise judgement here on when to use AI, and when we need to spend the time to understand what we’re trying to summarize, or to talk to people versus the temptation to ask AI to answer all the questions for us. On the management side, we’re ultimately accountable for these decisions, and this is the same on the engineering IC side, so it is important to still keep those skills sharp.


**Specializations still matter even in a world where code is cheap.** I had some great conversations with others in the mobile space about how we’re thinking about mobile specialists and mobile app development. I’ve long been a believer that leaning into these platform specialists and native apps produces higher quality experiences for users. With AI reducing the time to produce code, it reinforces why native investment still pays off.


### Rebecca Borison, Retirement Engineering Manager


Not surprisingly, a lot of the talks this year revolved around how to better work with AI, but it was super interesting to hear how other companies were thinking through the same challenges we’re seeing at Gusto.


Here are a few of the things that stuck with me:


**Speed without judgement is just risk.** Some parts of a system are fine to move fast and loose on: UI, boilerplate, low-stakes experiments. Others need a human slowing things down on purpose: anything touching money, security, or decisions that are hard to unwind. The question isn’t “should we use AI to go faster,” it’s “where is going faster actually safe.”


**Output is not the same as impact.** This came up again and again, especially from engineering leaders being asked to justify AI spend: lines of code, tickets closed, and raw velocity are easy to measure and easy to game, and they don’t tell you whether the work actually helped anyone. The better question is whether friction went down for the people using what you built, and whether it moved something that mattered to the business. That’s true whether you’re an engineer, a designer, or a PM — it’s easy to feel productive without being useful.


**The skills that matter are shifting toward the human ones.** As AI takes over more of the routine work, the thing that’s left to us is understanding the real problem: talking to the people affected, having the context to know what “good” looks like, and using judgement about tradeoffs. The differentiator isn’t how fast you can produce something anymore, it’s whether you understood the problem in the first place.


### Vianca Martinez, Symmetry Software Engineer


We are all navigating the same challenges with AI. With a new way to “AI” every day, I often felt like I was behind; hearing others wrestle with the same questions around code reviews, developing the next generation of engineers, and adapting to a changing SDLC helped quiet some of that imposter syndrome.


My key takeaways were that as code becomes cheaper and easier to produce, the value of an engineer is shifting away from simply writing code and more toward planning, defining intent, setting the right guardrails, and **validating that we’re solving the right problems** . We’re moving toward an SDLC where specs and tests become increasingly important, agents are trusted to work through more of the development cycle independently, and our job becomes less about babysitting AI and more about **giving it the right context and tools to succeed.**


Another interesting tension was around the next generation of engineers. Junior software engineering hiring is declining industry-wide., yet we’ll still need to cultivate the next generation of strong, AI-native engineers who can eventually become our senior engineers and technical leaders. If AI is changing how engineers learn and gain experience, then we also have to **rethink how we create those opportunities** and develop strong engineering judgement along the way.


Most importantly, AI fluency isn’t about keeping up with every new tool; it’s about learning how to adapt our engineering practices around it.


### Anshuma Chandak, Senior Staff AI/ML Engineer


**Reality check: LLMs are powerful, but the workflow matters**


One of the clearest themes was a more grounded understanding of LLM limits. Because outputs are stochastic, they’re hard to trust for deterministic decision-making. Instead, the more durable pattern is using AI to build tools and workflows that help people make better decisions. This is better than treating “agentic AI” as something that should run wild and autonomously figure everything out.


**Context remains the hardest unsolved piece**


Many teams still don’t have a settled best practice for giving models the right context. It is not uncommon to see teams leaning on brute-force approaches like putting large amounts of text into the context window. There isn’t yet a consistent definition of what “good context” looks like or how to make it reliable and repeatable.


**Impact is shifting from activity metrics to outcomes**


There was also a noticeable move away from measuring engineering productivity through proxies like PR count or tokens consumed. More organizations are asking teams to connect work to outcomes like what changed for users or the business, since raw activity is easy to optimize (and game) without necessarily creating meaningful impact.


### Irina Khafizova, Gusto Pro Engineer


**Key takeaways from LeadDev**


**AI makes code cheaper, so engineering judgement, context, and guardrails matter more.** A lot of the conversation was about shifting review and rigor upstream, turning repeated learnings into systems, and keeping business context (and knowledge sharing) front and center.


- **Review decisions, not just diffs.** Push review earlier: intent, acceptance criteria, architecture, assumptions, and tradeoffs. Treat the PR as evidence of decisions, not the decision record.
- **Automate recurring feedback.** Turn “we always comment on this” into a test, lint rule, constraint, agent instruction, or automated check.
- **Scale autonomy with risk.** Decide how much autonomy is OK based on blast radius, reversibility, error tolerance, and cognitive complexity.
- **Use multiple agents to surface ambiguity.** Independent proposals/reviews can highlight disagreements — often the signal that requirements or assumptions are unclear.
- **Preserve knowledge sharing.** Reviews and pairing also build shared understanding; don’t automate that benefit away.
- **Lean on domain knowledge.** As implementation gets easier, “why this exists” (constraints, failure modes, history, what matters) becomes a bigger part of impact.
- **Match rigor to risk.** Not every change needs the same process; calibrate with complexity, potential damage, reversibility, and failure tolerance.
- **Anchor technical choices in business context.** The “best” technical solution isn’t always the right one; weigh value, cost, and opportunity cost.


**TL;DR**


**AI changes where we spend time, not the need for judgement.** Let automation handle more implementation and repetitive verification; keep humans focused on intent, architecture, risk, and the decisions behind the code.


### Alyssa Hester, Senior Staff Consumer Money Engineer


**Documentation for the win**


In a world where the implementation details matter less, the what, the why and the core non-functional system requirements become more important. Clear, crisp documentation is required, now more than ever. We can lean into documentation to validate system correctness and user experience as we continue to build rapidly with agents. Documentation preserves decision history and reasoning, something quickly lost within code given the new rate of change.


**Fundamentals aren’t going away**


We should continue focusing on improving our core platform including guard rails, CI/CD, and other platform work. This helps humans *and* agents. Test driven design, listing system invariants to clearly state what a system should do, and leaning in to domain driven design can both help us think more clearly and provide context for agents that leads to better results.


**Be open to experimentation**


How we work has to change. There won’t be a one size fits all model but we should continue to embrace curiosity, dropping ways of working that no longer serve us. Be willing to try something new.


**30 min MBA summary — a non AI talk**


One talk focused on summarizing an executive MBA program to thirty minutes. I’ll summarize even further to just one point: think of engineering work and technical projects as investments. As engineers we often understand the importance on a low level, but how does this translate into business health? Going through this exercise can help align engineering with other stakeholders and create tangible business impact.


*📸 Pictured left to right: Tori Huang, Alyssa Hester, doing NYC stuff after Day 1 at the conference*


### Tori Huang, Senior Staff Payroll Engineer


Hello, it’s me again.


My teammates have covered the bases. We learned everything from practical advice on working with AI in our day to day, trends in where tech is heading, and how to continue to stay ahead of these changes.


The biggest takeaway for me was: the only guarantee over the next six months is more change. In the midst of all these transformations, we need people to guide us at every level. It was pretty cool to be there with a bunch of other people learning how to be better leaders for their teams.


If you are one of these people, or simply trying to navigate how quickly our industry is changing, LeadDev is worth attending. You’ll leave with new ideas, connections, and fresh energy for what comes next. Thanks for an awesome time, LeadDev, hope to see you at the next one! 💖
